record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.original_question: How can detailed atmospheric abundance measurements of giant and intermediate-mass exoplanets, combined with host-star properties and planetary mean densities, clarify the nature of gaseous-rich planets with masses and sizes comparable to Uranus and Neptune?

evidence.quote: Given this fact, and ubiquity of similar-mass planets in other planetary systems, it is essential to understand their interior structure and composition.
Detailed and accurate measurements of atmospheric abundances of giant and intermediate-mass exoplanets will also be valuable.

An overview of the variation in atmospheric composition of gaseous exoplanets in the mass/size range of Uranus and Neptune, and its connection to the host star's properties, in concert with determinations of the planetary mean density will allow us to understand the nature of gaseous-rich intermediate mass planets.

artifact.category_tag: exoplanet atmospheric composition and interior structure
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of gaseous-rich exoplanets whose masses and radii lie within the range spanned by Uranus and Neptune (roughly 14–17 Earth masses and 3.9–4.0 Earth radii, with bulk mean densities of order 1.3–1.6 g cm⁻³). For each such planet, suppose one can obtain: (i) detailed atmospheric abundance measurements (mixing ratios of H, He, C, N, O, S and selected heavier species, including metallicities relative to solar and key elemental ratios such as C/O and N/O), (ii) the elemental abundances and metallicity of the host star, and (iii) an accurate planetary mean density derived from independent mass and radius determinations.

Develop a quantitative framework that uses these three categories of observables jointly to constrain the interior structure and bulk composition of such intermediate-mass gaseous planets. Specifically, determine to what extent the combined dataset:

(a) distinguishes among competing interior models (e.g., differentiated rock/ice/H–He envelope models versus compositionally inhomogeneous or fully mixed models),
(b) constrains the bulk heavy-element mass fraction and the partitioning of heavy elements between atmosphere, envelope, and deep interior,
(c) tests whether the atmospheric metal enrichment relative to the host star follows a universal mass–metallicity relation analogous to that suggested for the Solar System giants, and
(d) clarifies the formation pathway (e.g., core accretion with planetesimal vs. pebble delivery, or gravitational instability) of planets in the Uranus/Neptune mass–radius regime.

Formulate the inverse problem precisely, identify the minimal set of observational precisions required for each input quantity to yield non-degenerate constraints on items (a)–(d), and characterize the residual degeneracies that cannot be broken by these data alone.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in planetary science concerning how exoplanet atmospheric abundances, host-star data, and mean densities together constrain interiors of Uranus/Neptune-mass planets. As of 2026 it remains an active area: JWST atmospheric spectra of sub-Neptunes and ice-giant analogs are being analyzed, and no definitive framework yet links these observables uniquely to interior structure. The question is open.
